![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/87182d625f4e669a6b2791a17f3e12c34922043b8f3deefd6b2473e8fb529886.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a section of the parabola $y=4-{x}^{2}$ from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(0,4).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

Let ${C}_{2}$ be the section of parabola $y=4-{x}^{2}$ from $A$ to $B.$ Then,
 $-{C}_{2}$ will be the same path but travelled from $B$ to $A.$ The path $-{C}_{2}$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t)=t\,i+(4-{t}^{2})\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<2.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=4-{t}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =x\,i=t\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2})j \\  & =i-2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i)\cdot (i-2t\,j) \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2-{\int }_{0}^{2}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{\int }_{0}^{2}t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2-[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$
